$comment: LoRaWAN through a network server's MQTT integration. The EMS never touches a radio here — the network server has already abstracted every gateway and every end node — so what is left varying is the topic tree, the downlink body, the uplink envelope and the payload layout, and all four are configuration. Two nodes behind ChirpStack, plus a third behind AWS IoT Core expressed as `custom` to show that a network server with no named profile costs three lines and no code. Byte offsets and field names below are invented: replace them with your node's payload documentation. Needs no extra dependency — paho-mqtt is already core.

connectors.$comment: The same connector against AWS IoT Core for LoRaWAN, whose topics are whatever IoT rule you wrote — which is exactly why it is not a named profile.
connectors.name: aws

devices.$comment: A submeter reporting a 32-bit kWh counter, instantaneous power, and packed status flags. `role` is what tells a generic node which field is its kWh total — guessing by field name would report 0.0 for the life of the deployment with nothing erroring. The battery_v field is gated to fPort 2: nodes multiplex payload layouts by port by design, and a field gated this way is carried forward from the last uplink that did carry it rather than being erased.
devices.name: grid_meter

devices.$comment: A relay node. Class A means this downlink is QUEUED until the node's next uplink — see connectors/lorawan.py's class docstring before wiring an algorithm to it.
devices.name: water_heater

devices.$comment: Behind AWS IoT Core: same device class, same field map, only the envelope paths differ. Three lines of config for a network server that has no named profile.
devices.name: remote_sensor
